subject: chemistry
title: Vitamins and enzymes in food
summary: How the structures of vitamins C and D explain their solubility, and how enzymes work as protein catalysts in digestion, including the effects of temperature and pH and the role of optical isomers.
body:
Vitamins are small organic molecules we need in tiny amounts, and enzymes are the protein catalysts that make digestion fast enough to keep us alive. Both topics come down to structure: the shape and polarity of a molecule decide whether a vitamin dissolves in water or fat, and whether an enzyme can grab hold of its substrate. This explains why boiling vegetables can strip out vitamin C and why cooking or acid can stop an enzyme working.

## Think of it like this

### "Like dissolves like" is like friendship groups at a school party

At a party, people tend to hang out with others who are like them. Water-soluble vitamins are like the outgoing people who mix easily with the water crowd: **vitamin C** has four –OH groups that form **hydrogen bonds** with water, so it dissolves readily. Fat-soluble vitamins are like the quieter group who stick to their own kind: **vitamin D** is a large, mostly non-polar molecule with only one –OH, so it mixes with fats and oils through **dispersion forces** instead. Being "in the water crowd" also explains why vitamin C is flushed out in urine and not stored, while vitamin D stays in fatty tissue.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* people choose their friends, but solubility depends on the balance of intermolecular forces, so a molecule with one small polar group and a large non-polar part still behaves mostly as non-polar.

### An enzyme is like a glove that moulds to your hand

The **active site** of an enzyme is like the inside of a glove, and the **substrate** is your hand. In the old **lock-and-key model**, the glove would be a rigid shape that only fits one exact hand. The more accurate **induced fit model** is like a snug sports glove that stretches slightly and wraps around your hand as you put it on, which in an enzyme puts strain on particular bonds in the substrate so they break more easily. Because only the right shape and pattern of polar, charged and non-polar groups fits, enzymes are highly **specific**, and the enzyme is released unchanged afterwards, just as you can take the glove off and use it again.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a glove just covers your hand, but an enzyme actively lowers the **activation energy** of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway, and it catalyses a chemical change in the substrate.

### Denaturation is like a melted plastic lunchbox lid

A lunchbox lid only clicks on if its shape is exactly right. Leave it on a hot car dashboard and it warps, and it will never fit again. Heating an enzyme above its **optimum temperature** does the same: the hydrogen bonds and other forces holding its tertiary structure break, the active site changes shape, and the substrate no longer fits. A pH far from the **optimum pH** has a similar effect by changing the charges on acidic and basic side chains, breaking ionic interactions. Cooling, though, is like putting the lid in the fridge: it just becomes slow and stiff but does not lose its shape.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a warped lid is damaged plastic, but a denatured enzyme still has all its peptide bonds; only its 3D shape is lost, and small pH changes can reduce activity without permanently denaturing it.

### In real life

Steaming or microwaving vegetables instead of boiling them helps keep more of their vitamin C, because less dissolves into the cooking water. Lactose-free milk is made using the enzyme lactase to hydrolyse lactose before you drink it, and aspartame in diet drinks shows how only one stereoisomer fits our sweet-taste receptors properly.

## Key ideas

### Vitamins and why they are essential

**Vitamins** are organic compounds needed in small amounts for normal body function. Many act as **coenzymes**: small non-protein molecules that some enzymes need in order to work.

A nutrient is **essential** if the body cannot make it (or cannot make enough of it), so it must come from the diet. A **non-essential** nutrient can be made by the body from other substances. For example, humans (unlike most other mammals) cannot make vitamin C, so it is essential for us. Vitamin D can be made in the skin when it is exposed to UV light from the sun, so people who get enough sunlight may need little from food, but people with limited sun exposure must get it from their diet or supplements. The same idea applies to amino acids and fatty acids: essential ones must come from food.

### Water-soluble versus fat-soluble vitamins

Whether a vitamin dissolves in water or in fat depends on its structure and polarity, following the rule 'like dissolves like'.

**Water-soluble vitamins** (vitamin C and the B vitamins) are small and contain many polar groups, especially –OH groups, that can form hydrogen bonds with water.

- **Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)**, C₆H₈O₆, is a small ring-containing molecule with four –OH groups and an ester (lactone) group. These form many hydrogen bonds with water, so vitamin C is very soluble in water.
- Consequences: water-soluble vitamins dissolve in blood plasma and are not stored in large amounts; any excess is removed in urine, so they are needed regularly in the diet. They leach into cooking water when vegetables are boiled, and vitamin C is also easily destroyed by heat and by oxidation.

**Fat-soluble vitamins** (A, D, E and K) are mostly large non-polar hydrocarbon structures.

- **Vitamin D** (for example vitamin D₃, C₂₇H₄₄O) is a large molecule with fused rings and a long hydrocarbon chain, and only one –OH group. The single –OH group cannot make up for the large non-polar part, so the molecule interacts with water poorly. Its main attractions to other molecules are dispersion forces, so it dissolves in fats and oils.
- Consequences: fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed along with dietary fat, are stored in fatty tissue and the liver, and are not easily excreted. They do not need to be eaten every day, but very large doses (usually from supplements) can build up to harmful levels.

| Property | Vitamin C | Vitamin D |
|---|---|---|
| Formula | C₆H₈O₆ | C₂₇H₄₄O (vitamin D₃) |
| Polar groups | four –OH, plus a C=O in the ring | one –OH |
| Main intermolecular forces with solvent | hydrogen bonds with water | dispersion forces with fats |
| Solubility | water-soluble | fat-soluble |
| Storage in body | not stored; excess excreted | stored in fatty tissue |

### Enzymes as protein catalysts

**Enzymes** are proteins that act as biological **catalysts**: they speed up reactions by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower **activation energy**, without being used up. They do not change ΔH for the reaction.

Each enzyme has an **active site**, a small pocket or groove formed by the tertiary (and sometimes quaternary) structure of the protein. The molecule that binds there is the **substrate**. Side chains lining the active site attract the substrate by hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and dispersion forces. The enzyme and substrate form an **enzyme–substrate complex**, the reaction happens, and the products are released, leaving the enzyme free to act again.

- In the simple **lock-and-key model**, the active site has a fixed shape that exactly matches the substrate.
- In the more accurate **induced fit model**, the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, wrapping more closely around it. This puts strain on particular bonds in the substrate, making them easier to break.

Enzymes are highly **specific**: each catalyses one reaction or type of reaction because only substrates with the right shape and the right pattern of polar, charged and non-polar groups fit the active site.

### Digestion

Digestion breaks large food molecules into small ones that can be absorbed into the blood. Most of these reactions are hydrolysis reactions catalysed by enzymes:

| Enzyme | Substrate | Products | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| amylase | starch | maltose (and glucose) | mouth and small intestine |
| protease (e.g. pepsin, trypsin) | proteins | smaller peptides and amino acids | stomach (pepsin), small intestine |
| lipase | triglycerides | fatty acids and glycerol | small intestine |

### Effect of temperature

As temperature rises from low values, reaction rate increases, because particles move faster and collide more often and with more energy. However, above the **optimum temperature** (about 37 °C for human enzymes), the extra energy disrupts the hydrogen bonds and other forces holding the tertiary structure together. The active site changes shape, the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme is **denatured**. The rate falls quickly. Denaturation by heat is usually permanent. At low temperatures enzymes are not denatured; they just work slowly, which is why refrigeration slows food spoilage.

### Effect of pH

Each enzyme has an **optimum pH**: about 2 for pepsin in the stomach, about 7 for amylase in saliva and about 8 for trypsin in the small intestine. Changing pH changes the charges on acidic and basic side chains:

`–COOH ⇌ –COO⁻ + H⁺`

`–NH₂ + H⁺ ⇌ –NH₃⁺`

In strong acid, –COO⁻ groups gain H⁺ and become neutral; in strong base, –NH₃⁺ groups lose H⁺. This breaks ionic interactions (and alters hydrogen bonds) that hold the tertiary structure, and changes the charges in the active site that bind the substrate. Moving away from the optimum pH reduces activity, and large changes denature the enzyme.

### Optical isomers and food

A carbon atom bonded to four different groups is a **chiral centre** (asymmetric carbon). A molecule with one chiral centre exists as two **optical isomers** (**enantiomers**), which are non-superimposable mirror images, like left and right hands. Enantiomers have the same physical properties (melting point, boiling point, solubility), but they rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions and they can behave very differently in the body.

All 2-amino acids except glycine (whose side chain is H, so two groups are the same) have a chiral centre. Proteins in living things are built almost entirely from one enantiomer of each amino acid. Because enzymes and taste receptors are themselves chiral, they interact with only one enantiomer properly, just as a right hand fits a right glove. This is why one enantiomer of a molecule can be an active drug or a strong flavour while its mirror image is weaker, different, or even harmful.

The artificial sweetener **aspartame** shows this. It is the methyl ester of a dipeptide made from aspartic acid and phenylalanine. Only the isomer made from the naturally occurring forms of both amino acids tastes intensely sweet; other stereoisomers are not sweet. Aspartame is about 200 times sweeter than sucrose, so only tiny amounts are used, adding very little energy. Because it contains a peptide bond and an ester bond, it slowly hydrolyses when heated, so it loses sweetness in baking. People with the inherited condition phenylketonuria must avoid it because it releases phenylalanine when digested.

## Worked examples

### Worked example 1: predicting vitamin solubility from structure

Vitamin A (retinol), C₂₀H₃₀O, has a ring and a long carbon chain with several C=C bonds and one –OH group at the end. Predict and explain its solubility.

Step 1, identify polar groups: one –OH only.

Step 2, identify the non-polar part: 20 carbons in a hydrocarbon ring and chain, by far most of the molecule.

Step 3, link to forces: the large non-polar part interacts mainly through dispersion forces. Hydrogen bonding from a single –OH is not enough to let it dissolve in water.

Step 4, conclusion: vitamin A is **fat-soluble**. It will be stored in fatty tissue and the liver rather than being excreted quickly.

### Worked example 2: interpreting enzyme data

The rate of starch hydrolysis by an amylase was measured at different temperatures.

| Temperature (°C) | 10 | 20 | 30 | 37 | 45 | 55 | 65 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Relative rate | 15 | 35 | 70 | 100 | 60 | 10 | 0 |

(a) Optimum temperature: the highest rate is at 37 °C.

(b) From 10 °C to 37 °C, the rate increases because enzyme and substrate molecules move faster, collide more often and more collisions have enough energy to react.

(c) Above 37 °C, the rate drops because the enzyme's tertiary structure is disrupted (hydrogen bonds and other side-chain interactions break), changing the shape of the active site so starch no longer binds. At 65 °C the enzyme is fully denatured.

(d) If the 10 °C sample is warmed to 37 °C, the rate rises to near 100, because cold does not denature the enzyme. If the 65 °C sample is cooled to 37 °C, the rate stays near 0, because heat denaturation is permanent.

### Worked example 3: finding a chiral centre

Which of these amino acids has a chiral centre: glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, or alanine, H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH?

- Glycine: the central carbon is bonded to –NH₂, –COOH, –H and –H. Two groups are the same, so it is **not chiral**.
- Alanine: the central carbon is bonded to –NH₂, –COOH, –H and –CH₃. All four groups are different, so it **is chiral** and has two enantiomers.

## Common mistakes

- Saying an enzyme is 'killed' at high temperature. Enzymes are not alive; they are denatured, meaning their 3D shape and active site are changed.
- Saying denaturation breaks peptide bonds. It disrupts the interactions holding the secondary and tertiary structure; the amino acid sequence stays the same.
- Saying vitamin D is fat-soluble because it 'has no polar groups'. It does have one –OH group; the point is that its large non-polar part dominates.
- Thinking low temperatures denature enzymes. Cold slows the reaction, but activity returns on warming.
- Thinking enantiomers have different boiling points or solubilities. Their physical properties are the same; they differ in how they rotate polarised light and how they interact with other chiral molecules such as enzymes.

## Exam tips

- To explain vitamin solubility, refer to specific functional groups, the size of the non-polar part, and the intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonding versus dispersion forces). Then link to storage in the body.
- For enzymes, use the full chain of reasoning: change in conditions → disrupted bonds or charges in tertiary structure → active site changes shape → substrate cannot bind → rate falls.
- Know the difference between the effect of heat on reaction rate (more frequent, more energetic collisions) and its effect on an enzyme above the optimum (denaturation).
- Be able to circle chiral centres on a structure, such as an amino acid or aspartame, by checking for four different groups.

## Tips to remember

- **"Like dissolves like"**: vitamin C (C₆H₈O₆) is small with four –OH groups, so it hydrogen bonds with water — water-soluble. Vitamin D (C₂₇H₄₄O) is a big hydrocarbon with only one –OH, so dispersion forces win — fat-soluble.
- **Fat-soluble vitamins are "A, D, E, K" — think "ADEK sits in the fat deck"**: they are stored in fatty tissue and the liver, so they can build up to harmful levels. Water-soluble C and B vitamins wash out in urine and must be eaten regularly. (Made-up rhyme.)
- **Boiling broccoli = a vitamin C tea you pour down the sink**: vitamin C leaches into cooking water and is destroyed by heat and oxidation.
- **"-ase" means enzyme, and the name tells you the food**: amyl**ase** → starch (amylose/amylopectin), prote**ase** → proteins, lip**ase** → lipids (triglycerides). All digest by hydrolysis.
- **Enzymes are "denatured, not dead"**: above the optimum (about 37 °C) or far from the optimum pH, the tertiary structure is disrupted and the active site changes shape — the substrate no longer fits. Cold only slows enzymes; activity returns on warming. Heat denaturation is permanent.
- **Chain of reasoning for enzyme questions**: change in conditions → disrupted bonds or charges in tertiary structure → active site changes shape → substrate cannot bind → rate falls. Quick self-check on chirality: every 2-amino acid except glycine (two H atoms) has a chiral centre.

## Key terms

- **Vitamin** — an organic compound needed in small amounts for normal body function.
- **Coenzyme** — a small non-protein organic molecule that an enzyme needs in order to work.
- **Essential nutrient** — a nutrient the body cannot make in sufficient amounts, so it must be eaten.
- **Water-soluble vitamin** — a vitamin with many polar groups that dissolves in water, such as vitamin C.
- **Fat-soluble vitamin** — a mainly non-polar vitamin that dissolves in fats, such as vitamin D.
- **Enzyme** — a protein that acts as a biological catalyst.
- **Active site** — the region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and reacts.
- **Substrate** — the molecule an enzyme acts on.
- **Induced fit model** — the idea that the active site changes shape slightly to fit the substrate as it binds.
- **Optimum** — the temperature or pH at which an enzyme works fastest.
- **Denaturation** — disruption of a protein's 3D shape so it can no longer function.
- **Chiral centre** — a carbon atom bonded to four different groups.
- **Enantiomers** — a pair of optical isomers that are non-superimposable mirror images.

## Summary

- Vitamins are needed in small amounts; essential ones must come from food because the body cannot make enough.
- Vitamin C has many –OH groups that hydrogen bond with water, so it is water-soluble and not stored; vitamin D is mostly non-polar, so it is fat-soluble and stored.
- Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy; the substrate binds at a specific active site (induced fit).
- Temperature above the optimum and pH away from the optimum disrupt tertiary structure and active-site charges, reducing activity or denaturing the enzyme.
- Molecules with a chiral centre form enantiomers; enzymes and taste receptors respond to only one, as shown by aspartame.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an enzyme?

options.A: A carbohydrate that provides energy for reactions in the body.
options.B: A protein that lowers the activation energy of a specific reaction without being used up.
options.C: A protein that increases the ΔH of a reaction so it releases more energy.
options.D: A vitamin that is consumed during digestion.

questions.explanation: Enzymes are protein catalysts that provide a pathway with lower activation energy and are not consumed. Option C is wrong because a catalyst does not change ΔH; it only changes the activation energy.

questions.prompt: A carbon atom is a chiral centre when it

options.A: is part of a C=C double bond.
options.D: is bonded to four different groups.

questions.explanation: A chiral centre is a carbon with four different groups attached, which allows two non-superimposable mirror-image forms. Being bonded to –OH (B) does not by itself make a carbon chiral; for example, the C–OH carbon in propan-2-ol has two identical CH₃ groups.

questions.prompt: Vitamin C is water-soluble while vitamin D is fat-soluble. The best explanation is that

options.A: vitamin C has many –OH groups that hydrogen bond with water, while vitamin D is mainly a large non-polar hydrocarbon with only one –OH group.
options.B: vitamin D has no polar groups at all.
options.C: vitamin C has a larger molar mass than vitamin D.
options.D: vitamin D forms ionic bonds with fats.

questions.explanation: Vitamin C's several –OH groups form extensive hydrogen bonds with water. Vitamin D's large non-polar part dominates, so it interacts mainly by dispersion forces and dissolves in fats. Option B is tempting but false: vitamin D does have one –OH group, it just is not enough to make it water-soluble.

questions.prompt: Why are people advised to eat foods containing vitamin C regularly, but not necessarily vitamin D every day?

options.A: Vitamin C is fat-soluble and is broken down in fatty tissue.
options.B: Vitamin D is destroyed by sunlight, so it cannot be stored.
options.C: Vitamin C is water-soluble and excess is excreted in urine, while vitamin D is stored in fatty tissue.
options.D: Vitamin D is a non-essential nutrient that the body never needs.

questions.explanation: Water-soluble vitamins are not stored and excess is removed in urine, so they must be replaced often; fat-soluble vitamins are stored in fatty tissue and the liver. Option D is wrong: vitamin D is needed, but the body can make some in the skin with UV light.

questions.prompt: Pepsin works in the stomach at a pH of about 2. When it passes into the small intestine (pH about 8), its activity drops sharply. The best explanation is that

options.A: the higher pH changes the charges on acidic and basic side chains, disrupting the tertiary structure and the active site.
options.B: the higher pH hydrolyses the peptide bonds in pepsin.
options.C: pepsin molecules move more slowly at higher pH, so there are fewer collisions.
options.D: the small intestine is colder than the stomach, so pepsin is denatured.

questions.explanation: Changing pH adds or removes H⁺ from side chains such as –COOH and –NH₂, changing their charges. This breaks ionic and hydrogen-bond interactions, altering the active site so the substrate no longer binds well. Option B is wrong: loss of activity from pH change is denaturation, which does not break peptide bonds.

questions.prompt: Two samples of the same enzyme are tested at 37 °C. Sample 1 was first kept at 4 °C; Sample 2 was first heated to 80 °C. Which result is expected?

options.A: Both samples work normally, because they are tested at the optimum temperature.
options.B: Neither sample works, because both were taken away from the optimum temperature.
options.C: Sample 1 does not work because it was denatured by cold; Sample 2 works normally.
options.D: Sample 1 works normally; Sample 2 has little or no activity because it was denatured by heat.

questions.explanation: Cold only slows an enzyme; its structure is unchanged, so activity returns at 37 °C. Heating to 80 °C disrupts the tertiary structure, and this denaturation is usually permanent, so Sample 2 stays inactive. Option C reverses the effect: low temperature does not denature enzymes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following amino acids does NOT have a chiral centre?
questions.explanation: Glycine's central carbon is bonded to two hydrogen atoms, so it does not have four different groups and is not chiral. Alanine, serine and valine each have four different groups on the central carbon (–NH₂, –COOH, –H and a non-H side chain), so each has a chiral centre.

questions.prompt: Aspartame loses its sweetness when used in baked cakes. The most likely reason is that

options.A: heating converts it into sucrose, which is less sweet.
options.B: heat in the presence of water hydrolyses its ester and peptide bonds, breaking it into molecules that are not sweet.
options.C: aspartame is fat-soluble and dissolves into the butter.
options.D: heat converts all of it into its mirror-image enantiomer, which is twice as sweet.

questions.explanation: Aspartame contains a peptide (amide) bond and an ester bond, which hydrolyse when heated with moisture, giving amino acids and methanol that do not have its intense sweet taste. Option A is wrong because aspartame is a dipeptide derivative, not a carbohydrate, and cannot turn into sucrose.
